transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-24 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Alicia Park (Redwood AE); Daniel Brooks (Redwood SE); Samir Patel (Nimbus - Lead ML Eng); Laura Chen (Nimbus - Infra); Miguel Torres (Nimbus - CTO)

[00:00] Alicia: Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. Quick agenda: Daniel will walk through the latest INT8/FP8 numbers, then we'll discuss quality checks and next steps for the staging pilot. Any additions?
[00:18] Samir: No, sounds good. I wanted to flag that our product team is also curious about worst-case tail latency, so if we can include 95/99p numbers that'd be great.
[00:28] Daniel: Yep, included. I have slides but I'll mostly call out the key deltas. Note: these are on our dedicated G5 nodes, batch sizes 1 and 8, sequence len ~512, KV cache enabled for the profile.
[00:38] Miguel: Quick question — are these using the same tokenizer? Last time we saw small diffs because of tokenization mapping.
[00:45] Daniel: Good call; we used the same tokenizer and pinned to model v1.3-hf. There may be minor tokenizer noise in auto transcriptions, but config is identical.
[01:10] Daniel: Okay so headline: INT8 gives about 2.1x tokens/sec vs FP16 baseline at batch=8 and about 1.6x at batch=1. FP8 (our experimental quant) sits between INT8 and FP16 on throughput but closer to INT8 on latency — about 1.8x at batch=8. Tail latency improvements for INT8: median down ~30%, 95p down ~22%, 99p down ~15% in our runs.
[01:45] Laura: That's promising. Any quality regressions we should worry about? Our use-case is product descriptions, a lot of factual detail, so hallucination is a big no-no.
[01:55] Daniel: Right — we ran automated evals on a calibration set (n=2k examples that mirror your production prompts). For INT8 we observed a small drop in ROUGE-L ~0.8 points on average, and BLEU-ish scores showed ~1% relative drop. FP8 had slightly better fidelity than INT8 on those metrics. But critical to note: the perceptual/semantic tests — human spot checks — flagged about 6% of INT8 outputs with subtle tokenization shifts that affected entity formatting.
[02:30] Samir: 6% is... borderline for us. Can we scope which prompts fail? Is it longer contexts?
[02:40] Daniel: Mostly longer contexts > 400 tokens and cases with lots of numerical entities and product codes. We think it ties to quantization noise in final layers. We're experimenting with selective layer FP16 for the last two layers to mitigate. That reduced regressions to ~1.5% in our internal runs but cost gains drop a little (INT8-with-selective-FP16 gives ~1.6x throughput not 2.1x).
[03:15] Miguel: OK that's an interesting tradeoff. We probably would accept selective-FP16 if it fixes entity issues. What about calibration — how many examples did you use to calibrate INT8?
[03:25] Daniel: We used 2k for the initial runs; when we bumped to 8k calibration examples the regressions dropped by another half. So calibration data matters a lot. For production we'd recommend at least 5k representative examples from your corpora, ideally including those numeric/product cases.
[03:50] Laura: We can put together 6k across categories. Any privacy concerns with sending sample prompts?
[03:58] Alicia: We will provide a secure upload link, and if you prefer we can run the calibration on the staging VPC so data never leaves your network.
[04:06] Samir: Staging VPC would be ideal. Laura, can you provision peering?
[04:11] Laura: Yes, I'll add that to action items.
[04:20] Daniel: On FP8: it's more experimental but gave a good middle ground — quality closer to FP16 in most semantics tests, with throughput that beats FP16 by ~60% but slightly under INT8. It handled numeric entities better in our test runs, probably due to better dynamic range.
[04:45] Alicia: Are there any runtime stability differences? Crashes, dequantization errors?
[04:50] Daniel: We saw no crashes. There were a couple of outliers on older CUDA driver combos where FP8 had perf cliffs; we documented driver matrix in the bench sheet. We'll share the exact driver/GPU combo we used.
[05:10] Samir: Can you walk through the rollback/fallback strategy if we see production regressions?
[05:16] Daniel: Sure — recommended approach: start with canary route (5-10% traffic) to INT8 quantized model with automatic quality monitoring. If evals cross regression thresholds, route back to FP16 or FP8. Redwood's smart routing can do automatic fallback per-route, and we can pin specific customer endpoints to FP16 while others use INT8.
[05:42] Miguel: How quick is the rollback in practice? Seconds, minutes?
[05:46] Daniel: It's near-instant for routing (seconds), but full confidence requires the eval window to run — we typically watch 1-2 hours of traffic for statistically meaningful signals.
[06:05] Samir: About monitoring — what signals should we look at? Token-level perplexity, divergence, direct NER exact-match?
[06:12] Daniel: We recommend a mix: automated perplexity / distribution shift, token confidence delta, and a small human-eval set focused on entities. Also track generation length anomalies and repetition. We'll ship suggested alert thresholds in the sheet.
[06:30] Laura: On infra — for the staging perf tests, do you need full dataset or sampled traces?
[06:35] Daniel: Sampled traces are fine for initial latency studies; for final QA we prefer full-ish distribution to catch rare edge-cases. For the 95/99p tail test we need realistic arrival patterns (burstiness) — we can simulate with your traces if you share them.
[07:00] Samir: We'll prepare traces. On the perf numbers, can you call out absolute latencies for batch=1? Roughly what's median/95/99 for INT8 vs FP16?
[07:15] Daniel: Sure — on the G5-like nodes, batch=1 median: FP16 ~120ms/token, INT8 ~85ms/token, FP8 ~92ms/token. 95p: FP16 ~210ms, INT8 ~165ms, FP8 ~175ms. 99p moves up accordingly, those were the earlier percentages I mentioned.
[07:38] Miguel: Nice. Cost delta estimates? We want to know unit economics.
[07:42] Daniel: Rough ballpark: INT8 can reduce inference cost per token by ~35-45% compared to FP16 depending on utilization; FP8 around 25-35%. We'll include a per-model cost calc in the spreadsheet with assumptions.
[07:58] Alicia: Anything about caching and batching interplay? We saw before that heavy KV-cache usage reduces per-token compute for long contexts.
[08:05] Daniel: Right — with KV cache enabled, effective per-token work for long streams drops and quantization benefits slightly amortize. For streaming scenarios INT8 improvements are still meaningful but a bit lower percent-wise because KV-cache already saves work. We'll provide plots showing batch vs sequence length deltas.
[08:28] Samir: On the human-eval front — do you have tips for how to design the spot-check? We want to catch subtle entity formatting and code-like outputs.
[08:36] Daniel: Recommended: 1) sample by intent and length, 2) include a dedicated numeric/product-code category, 3) blind A/B with FP16 baseline, and 4) record example failures verbatim. We'll provide a template for the spot-check.
[08:55] Laura: When you say "selective FP16 last two layers", is that something Redwood supports out of the box or is it a custom model recompile?
[09:02] Daniel: It's supported in our runtime as a config knob for select layers; we run a quick recompile step but it's an automated job on our infra. No model-source change needed.
[09:12] Miguel: That's convenient. Any thoughts on when we'd go to production INT8 vs keep FP16? Do you recommend a two-phase rollout?
[09:18] Daniel: Two-phase typically works well: internal canary -> limited customer canary -> ramp. Use selective-FP16 for the initial canary if you have high-entity content. If results are good, move to full INT8 for lower-cost endpoints.
[09:33] Samir: Let's talk about the concrete pilot plan. We want to run a 2-week pilot on staging: 1) run calibration with our 6k examples, 2) do canary traffic at 10% for 48 hours, 3) run human spot-checks and automated checks, 4) evaluate rollback. Does that timeline make sense?
[09:50] Alicia: Yes, sounds reasonable. We'll need network access and the calibration set. Daniel will provide the quant configs.
[09:58] Laura: I'll get peering set up this week.
[10:05] Daniel: I will also attach the bench logs and exact driver/GPU combinations. Expect bench sheet by Friday.
[10:11] Miguel: Anything else on compliance? We need to ensure logs/audit for the pilot.
[10:15] Alicia: We'll enable audit logs for the pilot and redwood can push S3 logs to your account or keep them in our control plane with access controls, your call.
[10:25] Samir: We'll prefer logs in our S3. Laura to coordinate with Alicia offline.
[10:31] Laura: noted.
[10:35] Daniel: Quick note — we found a small tokenizer mismatch in one early run, so please pin the tokenizer hash we include in the sheet. Tokenizer differences can look like quantization regressions.
[10:48] Samir: Good to know.
[10:51] Alicia: OK let's recap next steps: Alicia share bench sheet + quant configs by 2/26; Laura share peering details by 2/28; Samir run the n=100 prompt quick check and a larger n=1000 internal sweep, report back by 3/3; Daniel to schedule tail-latency test on 3/1. Anything missing?
[11:09] Miguel: Can we get an explicit escalation path if we hit a blocking regression?
[11:14] Alicia: Yes — Alicia (AE) -> Daniel (SE) -> Redwood on-call infra. We'll include contacts in the doc.
[11:21] Samir: Perfect. Thanks all.
[11:25] Alicia: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with links and sheets.

Notes: occasional auto-transcription errors present in earlier bench filenames (e.g., "Run:m" vs "Run:me"). Recorded audio had slight overlap near 00:20 when multiple participants chimed.

End of transcript.
